beads.title: The notify stream carries no session identity, so the daemon cannot own a foreground serve
beads.description:
Two fields are missing from every frame this daemon puts on the notify bus, and the second one is holding a whole subsystem down.

In `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`, `WatchNotificationsAs` mints one id per subscription -- `sessionID := rands.HexString(16)` -- and does two things with it. It sets it on the first frame as `Notify.SessionID`, but only when the watcher asked for `NotifyInitialState`; the field's own doc tells clients to store it, because no later frame repeats it. And it registers `defer b.DeleteForegroundSession(sessionID)` for the life of that watch. The consumer is foreground `serve`. In `cmd/tailscale/cli/serve_v2.go`, a foreground `serve`/`funnel` opens `watcher, err = e.lc.WatchIPNBus(ctx, ipn.NotifyInitialState)`, reads exactly one notify, refuses outright with `errors.New("missing SessionID")` if the field is empty, and then installs its nested config at `mak.Set(&sc.Foreground, n.SessionID, fsc)`. `ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go`'s `DeleteForegroundSession` deletes exactly that key. So upstream's foreground serve is torn down by the DAEMON, and it survives nothing: not a `SIGKILL` of the CLI, not a lost SSH session, not a laptop lid. The CLI does not have to be alive, or well-behaved, or given a chance to run a handler.

The other field is `Notify.Version`. `sendToLocked` fills it unconditionally on the way out (`if n.Version == "" { n.Version = version.Long() }`), so every frame a watcher receives states which backend produced it -- which matters for a bus whose field set is explicitly not a stable API.

This fork has neither. `NotifyView` (`src/localapi.rs`) carries `state`, `error`, `browse_to_url`, `net_map`, `prefs` and `policy`, and nothing that identifies the session or the daemon. The consequence is already written down in two places as a deviation rather than a gap: `docs/PARITY_GAP_ANALYSIS.md` records that a killed foreground `tnet serve` leaves its serve installed until `tnet serve reset`, because `tnet` restores the previous config from its own `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` handler (`hold_foreground_serve` in `src/bin/tnet.rs`), and `src/ipn/serve.rs` says in its own docs that `ServeConfig.Foreground` is not modelled -- which is also why two of Go's serve refusals (`listener already exists for port %d` and `foreground listener already exists for port %d`) have no counterpart. All of that traces to one missing string on one frame.

DECISIONS. FIRST, scope this bead to the two frame fields and NOT to `ServeConfig.Foreground`: the session id is the primitive, the foreground config model is a separate and much larger piece of work, and filing them together would produce a branch nobody can review. Emit `session_id` on the first frame of a masked watch (Go gates it on `NotifyInitialState`; this fork's nearest equivalent is `initial_state`, and copying Go's gate keeps the contract identical) and `version` on every frame. SECOND, what the id is: Go uses 16 hex chars from its own RNG, and the value is opaque to the client, so any collision-resistant per-connection identifier is faithful -- but it must be stable for the life of the connection and must NOT be reused across connections, because it will later key server-side state. THIRD, say in the request's rustdoc that the id is not yet load-bearing, so the next reader does not assume a foreground serve is already tied to it.

beads.title: A watcher cannot subscribe to a status snapshot, so it must open a second connection and race it
The exit-node suggestion never reaches the notify bus, so a watcher polls for a value the daemon already has
beads.description:
Upstream puts the suggestion on the bus twice: once when a watcher subscribes and once whenever the answer changes.

The front-load is `NotifyInitialSuggestedExitNode` (`1 << 10`): in `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`'s initial-notify assembly, `if en, err := b.suggestExitNodeLocked(); err == nil { ini.SuggestedExitNode = &en.ID }` -- a bare `tailcfg.StableNodeID`, nothing more.

The ongoing half is not a separate watcher and not a timer; it lives inside `suggestExitNodeLocked` itself. That function captures `prevSuggestion := b.lastSuggestedExitNode`, computes the new pick from the preferred DERP, the per-region latency map, the route-check report and `b.getAllowedSuggestions()`, and then:

    if prevSuggestion != res.ID {
        // Notify the clients via the IPN bus if the exit node suggestion has changed.
        b.sendToLocked(ipn.Notify{SuggestedExitNode: &res.ID}, allClients)
    }
    b.lastSuggestedExitNode = res.ID

Three properties come from that placement and all three are worth keeping. The push is change-triggered, so a stable answer costs nothing on the bus. It goes to `allClients` rather than to the session that triggered the computation, because the suggestion is a property of the node, not of the asker. And it fires wherever a suggestion is computed -- including the re-run that `sysPolicyChanged` performs after `AllowedSuggestedExitNodes` moves, so an administrator's edit re-picks and every watcher is told, without anyone asking.

This fork computes the same value and will only give it up on request. `Backend::suggest_exit_node` (`src/ipn/mod.rs`, over `diag::suggest_exit_node`) answers `Request::SuggestExitNode` with a `Response::ExitNodeSuggestion`, and since the `AllowedSuggestedExitNodes` work the pick is already filtered through the administrator's allow-list -- so the value is present and already policy-correct. It is simply unreachable from a `watch`. `docs/PARITY_GAP_ANALYSIS.md` has been listing `SuggestedExitNode` among the absent notify fields for several editions without ruling on it; the ranking work that made the suggestion hard belongs to the engine, and the notification does not.

DECISIONS. FIRST, where the last-suggestion cell lives: Go keeps `lastSuggestedExitNode` on the backend and compares inside the compute function, which is the only placement that cannot drift from the value actually returned -- put it on `Backend` and push from `suggest_exit_node`, not from the request handler. SECOND, this fork's suggestion is computed on demand and nothing else calls it, so unlike Go there is no netcheck-driven or policy-driven re-run to ride: the honest contract is "front-loaded on subscribe, and re-sent whenever a suggestion is computed and differs", which is narrower than Go's and should be written as such in the mask field's rustdoc rather than implied to be equivalent. Do not add a polling timer to close the difference; a timer that re-probes the engine on a schedule is a different and larger decision. THIRD, `Response::ExitNodeSuggestion` already models "no eligible candidate" and "excluded by the allow-list" as the same honest empty result -- keep that on the bus too, and decide explicitly whether an empty suggestion is a frame at all or silence (Go sends nothing when `suggestExitNodeLocked` errors, so silence is the faithful default).

beads.title: A watcher is told the peer set changed and never that its own node did
beads.description:
`Notify.SelfChange` is one of the few fields upstream does NOT gate behind a mask bit, which is a statement about how basic it considers it. In `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`, every netmap update builds it:

    var selfChange *tailcfg.Node
    if st.NetMap.SelfNode.Valid() {
        selfChange = st.NetMap.SelfNode.AsStruct()
    }
    notify := ipn.Notify{SelfChange: selfChange}

and the initial notify carries it too when `NotifyInitialNetMap` is set (`ini.SelfChange = nm.SelfNode.AsStruct()`). The field's doc says why it exists and names its consumers: it carries the new self node "so reactive consumers (containerboot, kube agents, sniproxy, etc.) can read the current self state without watching the full netmap", and tells anything needing more -- peers, DNS config, packet filter -- to react to it by fetching the netmap on demand. It was added as the scalable replacement for the bus `NetMap` field, which upstream has now marked deprecated and emits only on Windows.

It is also a session boundary rather than a plain field. `watchSession.lastSentSelf` records the self node last delivered to that session, with the comment "a change to self is a profile boundary for implicit bus state", and `selfChangeResetsImplicitState` resets the session's per-session dedup state (`lastSentUserProfile`) when that identity changes.

Here a watcher gets the opposite of the modern shape. `NotifyView::net_map` is `Option<Vec<PeerReport>>` -- the full peer set, every time -- and there is no self at all. So a `watch` tells a subscriber everything about every other node in the tailnet and nothing about the node it is running on: its own addresses, its MagicDNS name, its key expiry, its capability set. To learn that its own key is about to expire, a consumer has to poll `status` on a second connection, which is exactly the pattern `SelfChange` was introduced to retire.

Daemon-buildable, and the pieces are in reach. `Device::status()` returns a `self_node` and `Backend::status()` already projects it into `self_ipv4`, `self_name` and `self_ipv6`, so a self frame emitted alongside each netmap tick in `stream_notify` (`src/server.rs`) needs no new engine capability.

DECISIONS. FIRST, what "changed" means: Go re-sends the self node on every netmap update rather than diffing it, which is the cheap reading and the one a consumer can rely on -- do the same, and say in the field's rustdoc that a frame means "the netmap moved", not "self is definitely different". Diffing would be a silent behavioural difference from Go dressed as an optimisation. SECOND, what the field carries: Go sends a whole `tailcfg.Node`, and this fork has no equivalent view type for self. Either mint a small `SelfReport` (the fields `Backend::status()` already projects, plus key expiry once it is available) or reuse the existing peer view; pick one and pin it with a test, because a self view that grows field by field over several editions is how a wire type becomes unreviewable. THIRD, leave the `lastSentSelf` dedup-reset machinery alone -- it exists to serve `UserProfiles` on peer-change sessions, and this fork has neither, so porting it now would be porting a mechanism with nothing to protect.

beads.title: A notify watcher that falls behind is silently starved instead of being told and disconnected
The watch mask is four booleans, so Go's two subscribe-time refusals have nowhere to land
beads.description:
`serveWatchIPNBus` (`ipn/localapi/localapi.go`) takes the entire subscription as ONE parameter -- a decimal `mask` read with `mask.UnmarshalText([]byte(s))` -- and refuses three ways before it subscribes to anything.

A value that will not parse gets `bad mask` (400).

A mask containing `NotifyInProcessNoDisconnect` gets `NotifyInProcessNoDisconnect is only valid for in-process IPN bus subscribers` (400). The reason is in the bit's own doc in `ipn/backend.go`: it marks a subscriber that must not be disconnected for falling behind, so instead the PRODUCER blocks until it catches up -- possibly while holding the backend mutex. A LocalAPI client must never be able to ask for that, and this is where that is enforced.

And `ipn.ValidateNotifyWatchOpt` refuses `NotifyRateLimit` combined with any bit in `NotifyRateLimitIncompatibleBits` (`NotifyPeerChanges | NotifyNoNetMap | NotifyInitialStatus | NotifyPeerPatches`), with `NotifyRateLimit is incompatible with new-style IPN bus subscription bits %v`. The constant carries the rationale: those bits describe stateful delta streams, and randomly delaying or merging messages in one breaks the consumer's ability to maintain a coherent local view. The same validator runs again inside `WatchNotificationsAs`, where a failure is delivered as a terminal `ErrMessage` frame rather than an HTTP error, because in-process callers do not have a status code.

This fork spells the mask as named boolean fields on `Request::Watch` (`src/localapi.rs`): `initial_state`, `initial_netmap`, `prefs`, `policy`, each `#[serde(default)]` and each dropped from the wire when false so a bare `{"cmd":"watch"}` stays byte-identical for older clients. That is the better wire format in almost every respect -- it is self-describing, it cannot be mis-typed as an integer, and the dual-path bare/masked contract is pinned by a test. What it cannot do is refuse. An unknown bit is not a value the daemon can look at; it is a field serde ignores. A forbidden COMBINATION has no shape in which a caller can even express it, so there is nothing to rule on and no place to put the rule.

Today that costs nothing, because none of the bits with a refusal attached is offered. It stops costing nothing as soon as the surface grows, and it is about to: the other rows this sweep filed each add a field to this same request, and one of them (`NotifyInitialStatus`) is a member of `NotifyRateLimitIncompatibleBits`.

DECISIONS -- this bead is the decision, and it should land as a written ruling plus whatever small code it implies, not as a large refactor. OPTION A, keep the booleans and port each refusal as a cross-field check on the parsed request, in the same shape this fork already uses for Go's one cross-flag usage refusal ("can only be used with --exit-node"): the check moves from "is this bit set in an integer" to "are these two fields both true", the message stays Go's, and the wire stays readable. OPTION B, carry Go's integer mask as an additional field for wire compatibility, and validate it exactly as Go does. A is almost certainly right -- this daemon's LocalAPI is its own protocol and has never claimed byte compatibility with Go's HTTP LocalAPI, and B would mean maintaining two spellings of the same subscription forever. Whichever is chosen, record it in the `Request::Watch` rustdoc next to the back-compat contract already documented there, including the explicit note that this fork does not offer `NotifyInProcessNoDisconnect` at all and why (there is no in-process subscriber, so the bit has no meaning here), so the next reader does not file its absence as a gap.
